extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary and philosophical history/criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and critical principles for judging the writings and influence of 17th–18th-century philosophers, historians, and literary figures, emphasizing style, originality, method, and moral/theological consequences. The page argues for standards of balance between past and innovation, sound historical method, and appropriate stylistic tone for subjects like religion and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality should not reject the past
rubrics_metrics.description: It was the great object of his desire to be throughout an original thinker in the strictest and most perfect sense of the word. For this purpose he resolved to forget, once for all, every thing he had before known, thought, or believed, and to begin entirely anew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt total oblivion of predecessors: throwing aside the thread of inherited thought leads to destruction and the needless revival of old errors. Examples/anti-patterns: Descartes' attempt at entire originality produced ideas that were often merely new versions of predecessors; political innovators who discard historical institutions produce absurd results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and use of inherited thought/language
rubrics_metrics.description: Were it possible at pleasure to throw entirely and effectually aside the thread of inherited thought (by which we are ... connected through language,) the consequences ... could be no other than destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sound author/thinker should engage predecessors and inherited traditions rather than neglect them; borrowing (even unintentional) is inevitable and preferable to ignorant reinvention. Avoid treating past labour as unworthy of notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain mind-body relation satisfactorily
rubrics_metrics.description: It was supposed a merit of Descartes, that he drew so perfect a line between spirit and matter. It must, however, appear unquestionably somewhat strange ... that it should have been looked on as something so new ... the mode in which Descartes made his distinction was so unsatisfactory and merely mathematical, that no good resulted from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical distinctions (e.g., between intellect and body) must lead to intelligible accounts of their connection and mutual influence; avoid abstract/mathematical separations that generate inextricable difficulties and leave relations incomprehensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match style to subject (tone appropriateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be matter of some doubt, whether the splendour of such eloquence as his be altogether an appropriate vehicle for the truths of religion, whether the simplicity of our faith do not better accord with a more artless and unlaboured style of composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a style appropriate to the subject's nature: religious subjects often call for simplicity and artlessness, though in contested periods eloquence can be valuable. Avoid styles that obscure or corrupt the substance (e.g., bombast) and be mindful when ornate language may misfit moral/religious content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve a medium between loftiness and artificiality
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is enclosed in a very narrow sphere, between two extremes, that of the lofty and sublime, and the merely artificial; its charm consists in the mingling of these two elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balanced style that mixes sublimity with refinement. Anti-patterns: poets too sublime may lack refinement and harmony; those too polished may lean to effeminacy and lack strength. Bossuet praised as a model who combines both without descending into bombast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast and inflated expression
rubrics_metrics.description: With the strictest purity and refinement ... he is master, whenever his subject requires it, of a greatness and sublimity which he never suffers to swell into the bombast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain grandeur without excess; monitor for passages that verge on rhetorical inflation which undermine seriousness and truthfulness of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style should enhance and convey moral and sublime truths
rubrics_metrics.description: They are not only examples of perfect style and expression, but also rich fountains of the most sublime and salutary truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond formal elegance, a writer's style should serve to communicate and reinforce moral or theological insights. Evaluate prose for its capacity to elevate thought, not merely to please linguistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate tone when writing on religion (avoid levity/sarcasm)
rubrics_metrics.description: He disdains none of the tricks of that dangerous art ... He employed his genius in a very culpable manner, when he set the example of writing concerning religion in the tone of apparent levity and bitter sarcasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating religious matters with sarcastic wit or apparent levity; such tactics may do violence to truth and can be used by later critics to undermine faith. Pascal's model became dangerous when copied for irreligious ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain philosophical consistency and avoid opportunism
rubrics_metrics.description: In Voltaire, indeed, there is no such thing to be found as any regular system of infidelity, scarcely even a single firm principle ... as the sophists of antiquity took a pleasure in showing the versatility ... so Voltaire wrote one book in favour and another in contradiction of Providence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer coherent, principled argumentation to toggling positions for effect; inconsistency undermines credibility and can mask personal bias or rhetorical convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not misuse scientific knowledge to denigrate higher truths
rubrics_metrics.description: It is singular with what a perversity of genius this man makes use of all the marvellous greatness of nature ... not for the purpose of exalting the character of the Creator, but for lowering that of men ... the eighteenth century ... made no use of the physical knowledge it inherited ... except one extremely hostile to the higher truths of religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply scientific and physical discoveries in ways that respect their proper philosophical and theological implications; avoid rhetorical moves that use natural science solely to belittle humanity or belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical composition should aim beyond anecdote
rubrics_metrics.description: The abundance of historical memoirs ... had increased to such a degree, that they might almost be said to be a proper literature by themselves ... they are, after all, only the harbingers and materials of history, not histories, in the proper acceptation of the word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Histories should synthesize materials into unified, original national or classical accounts rather than fragment into conversational anecdotes. Evaluate historical works for unity, scope, and methodological rigor (compare to Machiavelli, ancient historians, or Hume and Robertson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal bias and national vanity in history
rubrics_metrics.description: It is evidently his purpose to make us believe that all the ages before that of Lewis XIV. were ages of darkness, and that even then, all nations except his were mere hordes of barbarians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historians should not let personal or national vanity reshape the past into a teleological narrative praising a favored era; beware of casting entire prior ages as darkness to exalt the present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide guiding unity and standards in political thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu ... neglected to give any rule or standard of unity to that immense collection of admirable political remarks and opinions which he laid before the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political analysis and collections of political observations should be organized under explicit guiding principles or standards; otherwise the result may be a drift of opinion without anchor (a ship without anchor or compass).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and philosophical inquiry requires profound, accurate method
rubrics_metrics.description: How much was set in a false light, how greatly historical truth was injured, ... begins now to be discovered, since historical inquirers have adopted a more profound and accurate method of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer deep, accurate research methods over taking facts on trust or relying on anecdotal authority; methodological rigor leads to correction of falsifications and prejudices about past ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical systems should not reduce all knowledge to the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: It is quite evident that no higher kind of belief or hope can obtain a place, where everything is enclosed within the narrow limits of the senses, and their experience ... The doctrine that the only true knowledge is that shaped out by the senses and experience ... is in general decided, although not openly expressed, materialism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating epistemological positions, check whether they leave room for higher belief or confine thought to sensory experience; an exclusively empirical account risks sliding into materialism and eliminating theological/moral horizons.
